Hi Mark, and thank you for reaching out. If you are indeed the Mark Pilgrim, I want to say sincerely that chardet (and Dive Into Python) had an enormous impact on my career and on the Python ecosystem. I've been the primary maintainer and contributor to this project for >12 years and I don't take that stewardship lightly.

I want to address your concerns directly.

**The core claim: that this is not a clean-room implementation and therefore must remain LGPL.**

I understand the concern, and I think it's worth engaging with seriously. You're right that I have had extensive exposure to the original codebase: I've been maintaining it for over a decade. A traditional clean-room approach involves a strict separation between people with knowledge of the original and people writing the new implementation, and that separation did not exist here.

However, the purpose of clean-room methodology is to ensure the resulting code is not a derivative work of the original. It is a means to an end, not the end itself. In this case, I can demonstrate that the end result is the same — the new code is structurally independent of the old code — through direct measurement rather than process guarantees alone.

I ran [JPlag](https://github.com/jplag/JPlag) v6.3.0 across every major release tag in this repository. JPlag parses Python source into syntactic tokens (function definitions, assignments, control flow, etc.), discarding all variable names, comments, whitespace, and formatting, then finds maximal matching subsequences using Greedy String Tiling. Renaming variables or reformatting code does not change the score.

| Version Pair             | Avg Similarity | Max Similarity |
| ------------------------ | -------------: | -------------: |
| 5.2.0 vs 5.0.0           |         90.93% |         93.83% |
| 5.0.0 vs 4.0.0           |         87.41% |         91.99% |
| 4.0.0 vs 3.0.0           |         82.99% |         94.09% |
| 2.2.0 vs 1.1             |         79.58% |         80.09% |
| 3.0.0 vs 2.2.0           |         34.87% |         43.01% |
| 6.0.0.post1 vs 5.2.0     |          3.30% |         80.05% |
| 1.1 vs 7.0.0             |          0.50% |          0.64% |
| **7.0.0 vs 6.0.0.post1** |      **0.04%** |      **1.29%** |

I want to draw attention to a critical distinction in this data. Version 6.0.0 had major changes to how the single-byte charset detectors were trained and stored, and that version shows only 3.3% average similarity to 5.2.0, but its **max similarity of 80%** tells you that entire files were carried forward from the prior release. It was still clearly part of the same lineage, still a derivative work, and still rightfully LGPL.

Version 7.0.0 is qualitatively different. Its max similarity against every prior version is under 1.3%. No file in the 7.0.0 codebase structurally resembles any file from any prior release. The matched tokens are common Python patterns that appear in any project: `argparse` boilerplate, `dict` literals, `import` blocks. This is not a case of "rewrote most of it but carried some files forward." [Nothing was carried forward.](https://github.com/chardet/chardet/commit/7e25bf40bb4ae6884892c094080e011290494947)

**On the LGPL's scope:**

I'm not a lawyer, but my understanding of the LGPL is that its copyleft provisions apply to derivative works (code that is derived from the licensed code) and do not extend to independent implementations of the same idea. Character encoding detection via BOMs, statistical modeling, and candidate elimination are well-established techniques described in [publicly available research](https://www-archive.mozilla.org/projects/intl/universalcharsetdetection) predating both uchardet and chardet. My understanding is that these ideas are not copyrightable expression, and that reimplementing them independently does not create a derivative work.

I'd also note that if prior exposure alone were enough to disqualify a rewrite, it would be very difficult for any maintainer of an LGPL project to ever write a new implementation of the same functionality under a different license, regardless of how different the resulting code is. I don't believe that's what the LGPL requires, but I'm open to hearing a different interpretation. The core question, as I see it, is whether the new work is derived from the old work, and the evidence above suggests that it is not.

**The process:**

For full transparency, here's how the rewrite was conducted. I used the [superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) brainstorming skill to create a [design document](https://github.com/chardet/chardet/commit/f51f523506a73f89f0f9538fd31be458d007ab93) specifying the architecture and approach I wanted based on the following requirements I had for the rewrite (I wrote these in Notes on my phone and don't have them committed in the repo, but I share them here for context):

> 1. Public API compatibility
> 2. Should still be called chardet, as the plan is to replace chardet
> 3. Not based on any GPL or LGPL code
> 4. High chardet detection accuracy on [test data](https://github.com/chardet/test-data)
> 5. Language detection _not_ a hard requirement, but if it is easy or a byproduct of other design, do it
> 6. Fast and memory efficient: should use multiple cores efficiently
> 7. No runtime dependencies
> 8. Must work on PyPy and CPython
> 9. Clean, modern design
> 10. If using trained statistical models, use data available via Hugging Face’s load dataset API
> 11. Any training code should cache data locally so we can retrain often during dev process
> 12. Benchmark often
> 13. Does not use tons of large dict literals that does not CPython 3.12 where it takes forever to import such things

I then started in an empty repository with no access to the old source tree, and explicitly instructed Claude not to base anything on LGPL/GPL-licensed code. You can see the history of all the design and implementation plans that were used to create 7.0.0 [here](https://github.com/chardet/chardet/commits/7.0.0.rc4/docs/plans?since=2026-02-26&until=2026-03-05&after=cc951583cf34e283b04e15942b1a053eb195c2cd+34). I did not write the code by hand, but I was deeply involved in designing, reviewing, and iterating on every aspect of it.

I understand this is a new and uncomfortable area, and that using AI tools in the rewrite of a long-standing open source project raises legitimate questions. But the evidence here is clear: 7.0 is an independent work, not a derivative of the LGPL-licensed codebase. The MIT license applies to it legitimately.

I'm happy to discuss this further, and I genuinely appreciate you raising the concern.

* The **state-machine logic and heuristics were reimplemented**, rather than copied.
* The **model loading and detection pipeline changed**, including different abstraction layers.
* The **code style and internal APIs differ substantially** from the earlier versions.

While both implementations solve the same problem (encoding detection), their **internal structure and organisation are not obviously derived from one another**.

**2. LGPL obligations depend on whether the work is derivative.**

LGPL restricts redistribution of *derivative works*, but it does not prevent independent re-implementations of the same techniques. Character encoding detection methods (statistical models, BOM detection, etc.) are well-known approaches and appear in multiple libraries.

If the implementation is genuinely independent, the LGPL’s copyleft provisions would not automatically apply.

That context matters when discussing why someone might reconsider architecture or licensing after maintaining infrastructure software for over a decade.

All previous releases remain available via the 6.x tags. Anyone who prefers the LGPL version can still use or fork that codebase.
